epithelial cells control the recruitment of neutrophils to the intestinal mucosa by releasing specific factors in a directional manner.

the role of epithelium in regulating the innate immune response to bacterial infection.
the mechanisms that regulate the recruitment of immune cells to mucosal surfaces.
how neutrophils are attracted to the gut and how epithelial cells direct this process.

the epithelial cells are the first line of defense in the gut and they are able to sense the presence of the pathogenic bacteria and they can release the specific molecules that can attract neutrophil to kill the pathogen.
the intestinal epithelium is a dynamic and active player in the immune response, capable of initiating and controlling the inflammatory response to luminal bacteria.

epithelial cells are not simply a physical barrier between the lumen and underlying immune cells but are actively involved in the initiation, regulation, and resolution of immune responses in the intestine.

the epithelial cells are the first responders to bacterial infection and are responsible for orchestrating the inflammatory response.
epithelial cells are not passive bystanders in the immune response, but rather active players in directing the immune response to the site of infection and controlling its intensity.
